title: Newton's Laws
body:
Three laws connect force to motion, and everything in the dynamics half of the course follows
from the second one.

**First law.** An object keeps its velocity, including a velocity of zero, until a net force
changes it. Motion needs no cause, and a change in motion does. A puck sliding on ice continues
because nothing significant opposes it.

**Second law.** The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration:

$$
\sum \mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}
$$

```
a net 20 N on a 10 kg block:   a = 20/10 = 2 m/s²
```

It is a vector equation, so it holds separately in each direction, and a
[[Free-Body Diagram]] is how the components get collected. The word net carries the
weight: the acceleration comes from the sum of every force, so an object with several large
forces that cancel does not accelerate at all.

**Third law.** Every force is one half of a pair, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction,
acting on two different objects. A book resting on a table is pushed up by the table and pulls
the table down. The two forces in the pair never appear on the same free-body diagram, because
they act on different objects, and confusing a third-law pair with two forces that happen to
balance on one object is the standard error.

Mass is the resistance to acceleration and is the same everywhere. Weight is the force gravity
exerts, $mg$, and changes with location.
